tagline.text: A multi-tiered limestone waterfall and emerald pools hidden in the Burgos forest

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: July–November, right after the rains when the flow is strong

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half a day to a full day

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,000 (entrance fee, tricycle hire and guide included; per person when 2–4 people share; bus fares excluded)

children.text: Kaangrian Falls is a multi-tiered waterfall in the forest of Barangay Agaga in Burgos, Ilocos Norte. You have to get past dirt roads and a short trek, but water spills in layers over broad rocks, making it a good fit if you want a quiet waterfall on the northwestern coast of the Philippines.

Kaangrian Falls is a waterfall in Burgos, at the far northwestern edge of Ilocos Norte. Wikipedia describes it as a multi-layered falls in Barangay Agaga, while a news report on a public road project places the same falls toward Paayas, so the barangay name differs by source. When you ask for directions locally, it is safest to say
Kaangrian Falls, Agaga
clearly in Burgos town proper. There is also a Burgos in Ilocos Sur, so be sure to add Ilocos Norte when you search in a map app.

The name is said to come from an Ilocano word meaning a foul smell. The usual explanation is the odor of bat droppings from nearby caves, but some visitors report noticing only fresh air. Assume the smell varies with the season and the wind, and don't worry too much about it. Despite the name, the falls themselves are clear water flowing down through green forest.

Rather than dropping in a single stream, the water spreads in many strands across rounded rocks and limestone steps, layer after layer. The upper tier is wide with small pools in a row, and a larger tier is said to lie below it. Getting down to the lower tier means gripping slippery rocks and tree roots, so decide based on your group's fitness.

The place is not as crowded as famous spots such as the Pagudpud beaches or the Bangui Windmills. The Ilocos Norte tourism office lists it as an official attraction with a ₱20 entrance fee, but signage and facilities are basic and the road is rough. It suits travelers who enjoy the walk through the forest to reach a waterfall more than a busy tourist site.

The signature view is the upper tier, where water splits into many strands across a wide rock face. When the flow is high the falls look much wider, and in the dry season thin streams reveal the patterns in the rock.

Below the falls, rocks coated with limestone deposits and small pools follow one after another. On clear days the water looks turquoise, but the depth is unknown, so don't jump in; test the water with your feet first.

Most of the trail to the falls runs under forest shade, so the sun is less of a burden even at midday. Some reports mention wild guavas along the path, and a few sections have concrete steps and metal railings.
The road from Burgos town proper to the trailhead passes farmland and hills. Bouncing along in a tricycle is part of the fun of a countryside trip in Ilocos.
A larger tier is known to lie below the first falls, but the way down is slippery and not recommended for everyone. Ask your guide about the current water level and rock conditions before deciding.
It is less well known than nearby Tanap-Avis Falls, and on weekdays you may have it almost to yourselves. That is lovely for listening to the water, but it also means help is not close by.

blocks.title: A day combined with Burgos sights

children.text: Kapurpurawan Rock Formation, Cape Bojeador Lighthouse and the Burgos Wind Farm are all in the same municipality. See the falls in the morning and move on to the coastal sights, and the day comes together nicely.

items.subtitle: From Burgos town proper to the falls

1–1.5 hours

Arrive in Burgos town proper, sign the visitors' list at the tourism office or municipal hall, and find a guide. Agree on the tricycle hire fee and the guide fee at this point.
Ride a tricycle along dirt farm roads to the entrance. Depending on road conditions it takes about

Walk from the entrance to the falls. Reports range from

Take photos on the upper tier and rest by the pools. When the flow is high, stay away from the water's edge and stay only where your guide says it is fine.
Walk back the way you came and ride the tricycle back to town. Have lunch in town or bring a packed lunch.
If you have time, stop at Kapurpurawan Rock Formation or Cape Bojeador Lighthouse. Both are close to the national highway.
The times are examples. They change with the first bus and how long it takes to find a guide, and in the rainy season you should adjust the plan after checking the forecast.

Ask the Burgos tourism office about a tricycle tour. Negotiate the fee in advance if you will visit both Kaangrian and Tanap-Avis.
Walk to Kaangrian Falls and enjoy the view. The tricycle driver often doubles as your guide.
Return to town for lunch, then pick one coastal sight, either Kapurpurawan Rock Formation or Cape Bojeador Lighthouse.
Head back to Pagudpud or Laoag before sunset. Dirt roads become dangerous after dark.
Rather than trying to see everything in one day, pick the falls plus one or two coastal sights and the day will feel more relaxed.

items.title: Walking from the entrance to the falls

children.text: Reports of the walking time range from
10–20 minutes
to about an hour. The difference seems to come from different starting points, so confirm with your guide.
There are forest paths, narrow streamside stretches and a stream crossing, and some sections have concrete steps and metal railings.
The last stretch is slippery with mud and wet roots.

Locals say the falls are fullest in the rainy season from July to November. One traveler who visited in dry April wrote that the flow was weaker than in the photos, but swimming was still possible. On the other hand, avoid days when it is actually raining, as the trail turns muddy and the water rises dangerously.

The best time is a clear day after several days of rain. One account from a visit after nearly two weeks without rain still described the current as somewhat strong, so after a typhoon passes, check trail and water conditions even more carefully.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: The flow is lower but walking is easy and it pairs well with the coastal sights.
The flow may be at its lowest, so bring water and enjoy the shade of the forest trail at midday.
The flow is rich, but avoid rainy days and the days right after a typhoon.

There is no lodging near the falls, so the practical approach is to stay in Laoag city or the Pagudpud beach area and visit as a day trip. Pagudpud has many beach resorts, and one record says the bus to Burgos takes about 30 minutes. Laoag has good air and bus connections and is convenient as a transit base.

Eat in Burgos town proper or bring a packed lunch. One account put lunch in town at about ₱50. Assume there are no restaurants near the falls and bring water, snacks and a garbage bag. A wider choice of restaurants is concentrated in Laoag and Pagudpud town.
Arrange your guide and tricycle together in town. Some accounts say the guide doubled as the tricycle driver.
Some accounts say you are asked to sign a visitors' list, so stop at the municipal hall or tourism office first.
Mobile signal is weak in places, so get your guide's number in advance and save the map offline.
Wear well-fitting shoes with good grip. Sandals are risky on mud and wet rocks.
Bring lunch and water. One account went without lunch and made do with cookies.
Carry plenty of small bills. They make it easier to split the entrance fee and the guide fee.
Take photos when clouds soften the sunlight; the rock patterns come out better.
Carry out all your trash. This is a quiet forest looked after by local residents.
On rainy days and right after a typhoon, the trail gets muddy and the water rises dangerously. Check the weather before you leave, and follow your guide if he or she tells you not to go.
Wet rocks and roots are very slippery. Go down to the lower tier only if you have enough stamina and proper shoes.
Do not jump or dive into pools of unknown depth. Ask your guide where swimming is allowed.
The current is strong when the flow is high. Keep a hand on children near the water.
Road works and dirt roads can make the trip slow, so allow plenty of time for the return and leave before dark.
The entrance fee, opening hours and whether a guide is required can change, so check for the latest information at the Burgos tourism office or municipal hall.
A white limestone coastal rock and Burgos's signature sight. It is easy to visit on the same day as the falls.
An old lighthouse on the Burgos coast with a great sea view. You can combine it with the falls in one day.
A row of coastal windmills that can also be seen from the Burgos Wind Farm. Easy to continue toward Pagudpud.
